\chapter{How Much Of It}
\label{ch:ml-degree}
\hlchaptermodality{79}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something is very good, really big or a bit small, instead of only good, big or small.}

From cold: both new degree words, which of them belongs in writing, the slot they stand in, and the third filler the learner already owned.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[vaḷare]{\ml{വളരെ} (vaḷare) — very}

\label{lesson:ML-C79-valare}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{good}. Say \emph{big}. Then say where either one stands when you put it with a thing-word, and what happens to its shape when you do.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വളരെ}}
\textbf{\ml{വളരെ}} — \emph{vaḷare} — very.

Since the chapter that gave you \emph{good}, \emph{big} and \emph{small}, you have owned five qualities and no way to grade any of them. A thing could be good. It could not be \textbf{very} good. This is the word that fixes that, and it costs nothing to use, because it works the way the quality words already work: \textbf{it stands in front, and nothing changes shape.}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{നല്ല}} \emph{nalla} & good \\
\textbf{\ml{വളരെ} \ml{നല്ല}} \emph{vaḷare nalla} & very good \\
\textbf{\ml{വലിയ}} \emph{valiya} & big \\
\textbf{\ml{വളരെ} \ml{വലിയ}} \emph{vaḷare valiya} & very big \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Look at the second column of that table and then at the first. \emph{nalla} is \emph{nalla} in both rows. English does the same thing — \emph{good} survives \emph{very good} intact — so there is nothing new to learn here beyond the word itself.

Now put a thing on the end of it and you have a three-word chain, each piece standing in front of the one it describes:

\textbf{\ml{വളരെ} \ml{നല്ല} \ml{പുസ്തകം}} — \emph{vaḷare nalla pustakaṁ} — a very good book.

Read that right to left and it unpacks cleanly: a book; a good book; a very good book. Each new word reaches forward over everything after it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five qualities, each of them now with a volume knob.

One word multiplied what five lessons gave you, which is what the small function words in a language tend to do.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vaḷare}
  \item \emph{vaḷare nalla}
  \item \emph{vaḷare valiya}
  \item \emph{vaḷare nalla pustakaṁ}
  \item what happened to \emph{nalla} when \emph{vaḷare} arrived in front of it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{vaḷare}? (\textbf{very}.) Does it stand before the quality word or after it? (\textbf{Before}.) And does the quality word change when it arrives? (\textbf{No.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[orupāṭŭ]{\ml{ഒരുപാട്} (orupāṭŭ) — a lot}

\label{lesson:ML-C79-orupadu}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{very good} out loud, and then say which of the two words in it you learned last.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{ഒരുപാട്}}
\textbf{\ml{ഒരുപാട്}} — \emph{orupāṭŭ} — a lot, a great deal.

It stands where \emph{vaḷare} stands and does the same job:

\textbf{\ml{ഒരുപാട്} \ml{നല്ല}} — \emph{orupāṭŭ nalla} — very good, a really good one.

The two are not interchangeable in feel, and the difference is one of register rather than of meaning. \textbf{\ml{വളരെ} is what a notice, a newspaper or a teacher writes.} \textbf{\ml{ഒരുപാട്} is what a person says to you across a table.} A learner who owns only one of them will be understood; a learner who owns both will sound like they have listened to somebody.

There is one thing \emph{orupāṭŭ} can do that a pure degree word cannot, and it is worth having: \textbf{it also measures an amount of stuff.}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{in front of} & \textbf{means} \\
\midrule
a quality word & \textbf{very} — \emph{orupāṭŭ nalla} \\
a thing word & \textbf{a lot of} — \emph{orupāṭŭ veḷḷaṁ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\ml{ഒരുപാട്} \ml{വെള്ളം}} is a lot of water. English needs an extra word there — \emph{a lot OF water} — and Malayalam needs nothing, because the word already sits in front of what it measures and that is the whole relationship.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two ways up, one for the page and one for the room.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{orupāṭŭ}
  \item \emph{orupāṭŭ nalla}
  \item \emph{orupāṭŭ veḷḷaṁ}, and say which of those two used it as an amount
  \item \emph{vaḷare nalla}, then \emph{orupāṭŭ nalla}, and say which one you would write down
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{orupāṭŭ}? (\textbf{a lot}.) Which of the pair belongs in writing? (\emph{\textbf{vaḷare}}.) And what does \emph{orupāṭŭ} mean in front of a thing rather than a quality? (\textbf{A lot of it.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[one slot, in front]{one slot, in front — three words that fit it}

\label{lesson:ML-C79-degree-slot}



\begin{quote}
Say the two new words of this chapter, and say what both of them did to the quality word standing after them.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the position, not the word}]
Both new words went in the same place. That place is the thing to learn, because once you can see it, a word you have never met can be dropped into it and you will know what it is doing.

\textbf{Immediately in front of a quality word, Malayalam keeps one open slot for how much.} Fill it or leave it empty; nothing else in the phrase reacts.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{slot} & \textbf{quality} & \textbf{what you said} \\
\midrule
— & \textbf{\ml{വലിയ}} & big \\
\textbf{\ml{കുറച്ച്}} & \textbf{\ml{വലിയ}} & a bit big \\
\textbf{\ml{വളരെ}} & \textbf{\ml{വലിയ}} & very big \\
\textbf{\ml{ഒരുപാട്}} & \textbf{\ml{വലിയ}} & really big \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the \emph{valiya} column downward. It is the same word in every row. \textbf{The slot carries all of the grading and the quality word carries none of it}, which is why one new word graded all five of your qualities at once rather than one of them.

The third filler is not new. \textbf{\ml{കുറച്ച്}} was handed to you as \emph{a little} for amounts of rice and water, and it stands in this slot too, at the small end — the same word, the same position, pointing down instead of up.

So the ladder is already complete, and two thirds of it were free:

\textbf{\ml{ഒരുപാട്} · \ml{വളരെ} · \ml{കുറച്ച്}} — a lot, very, a bit.

And the slot nests with the one you already know. The quality word stands in front of the thing; the degree word stands in front of the quality. Each piece reaches forward over everything after it, and nothing ever changes shape:

\textbf{\ml{വളരെ} \ml{വലിയ} \ml{പുസ്തകം}} — \emph{vaḷare valiya pustakaṁ} — a very big book.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A grade for every quality, and a place to put the next degree word you meet.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{valiya}, then the same word with each of the three fillers in front
  \item which filler you already owned before this chapter
  \item what changed about \emph{valiya} across all four of those phrases
  \item where the degree word stands, and where the quality word stands
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does a degree word go? (\textbf{Immediately in front of the quality word}.) What does the quality word do about it? (\textbf{Nothing — it does not change}.) And which of the three fillers points down rather than up? (\emph{\textbf{kuṟaccŭ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ethra enna ōrmma]{(how much of it) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R79-degree-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{very}, say \emph{a lot}, and say which of the two you would put in a letter.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one slot, three fillers, nothing else moves}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{filler} & \textbf{reading} & \textbf{where it came from} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഒരുപാട്}} \emph{orupāṭŭ} & really, a lot & this chapter, the spoken one \\
\textbf{\ml{വളരെ}} \emph{vaḷare} & very & this chapter, the written one \\
\textbf{\ml{കുറച്ച്}} \emph{kuṟaccŭ} & a bit & the short-answers chapter, already yours \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The slot sits \textbf{immediately in front of the quality word}, and the quality word never changes: \emph{nalla} is \emph{nalla} whether or not something stands before it.

Nest the two positions and the order comes out the same every time — \textbf{how much, then what kind, then the thing}:

\textbf{\ml{വളരെ} \ml{നല്ല} \ml{പുസ്തകം}} — \emph{vaḷare nalla pustakaṁ} — a very good book.

One of the three also measures stuff rather than qualities: \textbf{\ml{ഒരുപാട്} \ml{വെള്ളം}} is a lot of water, with no joining word between them.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Every quality you own, at three settings.

The five qualities were flat before this chapter — a thing was good or it was not — and two words turned each of them into a range. That is the return this language pays on small words standing in fixed places, and it is worth watching for: \textbf{when a word does not change shape, look at what stands next to it.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vaḷare nalla}
  \item \emph{orupāṭŭ valiya}
  \item \emph{vaḷare nalla pustakaṁ}
  \item \emph{orupāṭŭ veḷḷaṁ}, and say what \emph{orupāṭŭ} is measuring there
  \item the filler that points down rather than up
  \item what the quality word does when a degree word arrives in front of it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which degree word belongs in writing? (\emph{\textbf{vaḷare}}.) Which one do you hear across a table? (\emph{\textbf{orupāṭŭ}}.) Where do both of them stand? (\textbf{Immediately in front of the quality word}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
